summary.text: Zyra is a Python framework for modular, reproducible data workflows spanning import, processing, visualization, and export of scientific and environmental data. It is well-suited for multi-stage data pipelines but is not positioned as a real-time streaming system or interactive exploration tool.

details.text: Zyra organizes work into modular connectors (ingest), processors, visualizers, and utilities, supporting reusable pipeline building across acquire, process, and visualize stages.
The framework includes CLI commands, a Python API, and MCP Tools integration, with LLM-powered features (Wizard, narrative swarm, semantic search) available when providers are configured.
Zyra targets scientific and environmental data, with documented examples for connectors, processing, and visualization workflows.
Zyra is not designed for continuous real-time data streaming or interactive exploratory analysis without composing custom workflows.

If your use case requires LLM-powered workflow suggestions (Wizard) or semantic data discovery, confirm your preferred provider is installed and configured per the LLM Providers section.

summary.text: Terraviz is designed to be self-hosted by organizations like museums. The recommended first step is to visit the install console in a browser before touching any code — it sizes up the work, filters to the kind of node you want, and substitutes your specific values into every command.

details.text: There are three tiers to choose from: a Viewer node (globe plus the upstream catalog, about 30 minutes to set up, roughly $5 per month); a Publisher node (your own datasets and tours, the publisher portal, semantic search, events, and a blog, two to three hours); and a Publisher node with branded desktop builds (adds about one hour). A museum that wants to publish its own content would typically choose the Publisher tier.

Every path starts with forking the repository on GitHub. Cloning upstream directly fails late rather than early — nothing breaks until you have resource IDs to push and no remote of your own to push them to.

Prerequisites you need in place before running any automation include: a Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan ($5 per month), a domain on Cloudflare DNS, a GitHub account, Node.js 22 or later, Git with Git LFS installed, and a password manager for four values that are shown exactly once and cannot be retrieved afterward.

Most of the installation is automated through the setup script, but a small number of steps cannot be automated: connecting Cloudflare Pages to your GitHub remote (an OAuth flow), Zero Trust identity-provider onboarding, generating the node keypair, minting an R2 S3 API token, and your first SSO sign-in to become admin.

The self-hosting reference is in docs/SELF_HOSTING.md in your fork. Once you complete the install through Phase 5, your own node also serves its own guided setup page at your hostname followed by /setup, generated from your checkout rather than the upstream revision.

nextSteps.text: Open the install console at the address shown in the README (terraviz.zyra-project.org/setup) before cloning anything. Use it to decide which tier fits your museum, collect the prerequisite values listed under Phase 0 (account ID, node hostname, Git remote), and print the pre-flight sheet.

Fork the repository on GitHub, then run the prerequisites check with the manual flag of the setup script (npm run setup followed by the manual flag) to get the list of steps only a human can complete before automation takes over.
Keep a password manager open from the start — four secrets are displayed exactly once during the install and cannot be read back afterward.

summary.text: Yes. Orbit is designed to work with any OpenAI-compatible provider, including local servers such as Ollama, LM Studio, or llama.cpp. In the desktop app this works out of the box; in the web app there is a CORS constraint that limits direct local-network connections.

details.text: The README explicitly lists Local LLM support as a desktop-app feature: you can connect Orbit to Ollama, LM Studio, or any OpenAI-compatible server on your local network.
The LLM provider implementation is written to support any provider that speaks the OpenAI chat completions API, and the comment list includes Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, and vLLM by name.

Local servers such as Ollama and LM Studio typically do not set CORS headers for the desktop webview origin. The desktop app routes requests through the Tauri HTTP plugin to bypass this restriction; the plain web build uses native fetch and would be blocked by CORS when targeting a local server.
A blank or absent API key is handled gracefully: the provider skips the Authorization header entirely, which is the no-auth path that local servers rely on.
If the LLM is unavailable for any reason, Orbit falls back transparently to its local keyword engine, so the docent remains functional without any network or model connection.

nextSteps.text: To use a local model, configure Orbit with the base URL of your local server (for example the default Ollama address) and leave the API key blank. No key is required for Ollama or LM Studio.
If you are running the web build rather than the desktop app, direct connections to a local server will be blocked by the browser's CORS policy. Use the desktop app for reliable local-model support.
Check your installed desktop app version to confirm it matches the revision examined here, since the Tauri HTTP plugin path is a desktop-only addition.

records.question: What does TerraViz support for local LLM connections?

summary.text: TerraViz supports local LLM connections through Orbit. It allows connections to Ollama, LM Studio, or any OpenAI-compatible server on a local network. The desktop app stores API keys securely in the OS keychain and supports direct connections to local LLM servers.

details.text: TerraViz supports local LLM connections through Orbit, its AI digital docent. This feature allows connecting to Ollama, LM Studio, or any OpenAI-compatible server on a local network.

records.question: How should contributors document a missing Zyra workflow step?

summary.text: Contributors should document a missing Zyra workflow step by filing a Workflow Gap issue and following the provided template.

details.text: To document a missing Zyra workflow step, contributors should file a "Workflow Gap / Missing Command" issue using the provided template.
The issue template requires describing the existing CLI commands, the missing functionality, and the desired behavior, including an example usage.
Contributors should also propose an implementation plan, including steps to implement the core functionality, add tests, and ensure comprehensive docstrings.
All PRs that add CLI functionality should link to the related Workflow Gap issue and follow the PR template checklist.

nextSteps.text: Use the Workflow Gap issue template to report the missing functionality and propose an implementation plan.
